title: Shabbat
subtitle: The holiness of the seventh day
intro: Shabbat is the heart of Jewish life and one of the main topics at the beit din. In this section you will learn why Shabbat was given, how it is welcomed, spent and seen off, what the 39 categories of work are, and how the different movements approach Shabbat.

overview.why: Shabbat is the heart of Jewish life and the first thing that fills the Jewish week with holiness: it reminds us that the world has a Creator, and that a person is free and not a slave to their work. Shabbat restores peace, joy and meaning to the family, and gives the candidate a weekly rhythm of life according to the covenant.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din you will almost always be asked what Shabbat means to you personally and how you actually observe it: candles, kiddush, meals, refraining from work and from weekday activities according to the norms of your movement. Be ready to answer honestly and concretely — what time you light candles, where you go on Shabbat, what you find hardest.
goals: Explain why Shabbat was given: a remembrance of Creation, of the Exodus, and a sign of the covenant
Welcome Shabbat: light candles and take part in Kabbalat Shabbat
Hold the Friday night meal with kiddush and close Shabbat with havdalah
Understand the 39 melachot, muktzeh, eruv and the principle of pikuach nefesh
Distinguish the approaches of the movements and build your own practice

deeper.text: The chapter on Shabbat in Rabbi Hayim Donin's book “To Be a Jew” calmly explains the meaning of the day and how Shabbat is structured, from candles to havdalah. Read it after the first three lessons to put together the overall picture.

lessons.title: The meaning of Shabbat: Creation, freedom and covenant
keyIdeas: Shabbat is the seventh day of the week; the Jewish day begins in the evening, so Shabbat begins on Friday at sunset.
In the book of Shemot the reason for Shabbat is Creation; in the book of Devarim it is the Exodus from Egypt and freedom; kiddush mentions both meanings.
“Remember” (zachor) — active commandments: kiddush, meals, joy; “keep” (shamor) — the prohibition of work; women are obligated in both.
The Torah calls Shabbat a sign and an everlasting covenant between the Almighty and the people of Israel.
Shabbat rest is menuchah; kavod Shabbat is preparation, oneg Shabbat is delight in the day; melachah is not exertion, but creative work.

blocks.text: The seventh day of Creation

**Shabbat** (Heb. שַׁבָּת) is the seventh day of the Jewish week. The word comes from the root sh-b-t, which means “to cease, to stop.” Shabbat begins on Friday evening at sunset and ends on Saturday evening, when the stars appear in the sky. The Jewish day always begins in the evening — as it is said in the account of Creation: “and there was evening and there was morning — one day” (Bereshit (Genesis) 1:5). Therefore Friday evening is already Shabbat.

The Torah first speaks of the seventh day at the very beginning, in the account of the creation of the world. For six days the Almighty was creating the world, and on the seventh He ceased from creating. Note: the first thing the Torah calls holy is not a mountain, not a temple and not an object, but *time*. The philosopher Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel called Shabbat “a palace in time”: a Jew builds a sanctuary not of stone, but of the hours and minutes that he gives to the Almighty, to his family and to his own soul.

blocks.he: וַיְבָרֶךְ אֱלֹהִים אֶת יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתוֹ, כִּי בוֹ שָׁבַת מִכָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים לַעֲשׂוֹת
blocks.translit: Vayevarech Elohim et yom hashevi'i vaykadesh oto, ki vo shavat mikol melachto asher bara Elohim la'asot
blocks.ru: And G-d blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, for on this day He ceased from all His work which G-d created to make

blocks.text: These three verses (Bereshit 2:1–3, beginning with the word “Vayechulu” — “And they were completed”) are recited by Jews every Friday evening, in the prayer and in the kiddush over wine. In this way, every week, a person testifies: the world has a Creator, the world is not accidental, and time has meaning and a rhythm.

Shabbat is precisely the seventh day of the week, an eternal sign between the Almighty and the people of Israel (Shemot 31:16–17). The holiness is tied to this day of Creation: it is not moved to another day of the week. Even on a journey and in another country, a Jew waits for this very seventh day.
Two versions of one commandment

The commandment of Shabbat is the fourth of the Ten Commandments (in Hebrew, “Aseret HaDibrot,” “the ten utterances”). The Torah gives the Ten Commandments twice: in the book of Shemot (Exodus), in the account of the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai, and in the book of Devarim (Deuteronomy), where Moshe repeats them to the people before the entry into the Land of Israel. The wordings of the commandment of Shabbat differ in the two places — and in that difference lie the two main meanings of Shabbat.

blocks.he: זָכוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
blocks.translit: Zachor et yom haShabbat lekadesho
blocks.ru: Remember the Shabbat day, to sanctify it

blocks.text: Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Shabbat to the L-rd your G-d: you shall do no work, neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the L-rd made heaven and the earth, the sea and all that is in them, and on the seventh day He rested; therefore the L-rd blessed the Shabbat day and sanctified it.

In the book of Shemot the reason for Shabbat is **Creation**: a person rests because the Creator rested, and by this acknowledges that the world belongs to Him. In the book of Devarim the commandment begins with a different word and is explained differently.

blocks.he: שָׁמוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
blocks.translit: Shamor et yom haShabbat lekadesho
blocks.ru: Keep the Shabbat day, to sanctify it

blocks.text: …so that your male servant and your female servant may rest, as you do. And remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the L-rd your G-d brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm; therefore the L-rd your G-d commanded you to keep the Shabbat day.

Here the reason for Shabbat is **the Exodus from Egypt** and freedom. A slave does not control his own time; a free person can stop. Shabbat extends also to those who depend on you: workers, servants, even animals. This is the first legislation in history of a weekly rest for everyone, and not only for masters. That is why both meanings are mentioned in the Shabbat kiddush: Shabbat is “a remembrance of the work of Creation” and “a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt.”
“Remember” and “keep”

The sages of the Talmud said: “‘Remember’ and ‘keep’ were spoken in a single utterance” (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 27a; Shevuot 20b) — that is, the Almighty pronounced both words at the same time, which a human mouth cannot do. This idea entered the hymn “Lecha Dodi,” which is sung on Friday evening. From the two words, tradition derives the two sides of Shabbat:

items: **Zachor (remember)** — active commandments: to sanctify the day with words (kiddush in the evening and havdalah at its close), festive meals, beautiful clothing, prayer, Torah study, joy. The Talmud teaches: “Remember — over wine,” that is, kiddush is recited over a cup of wine (Pesachim 106a).
**Shamor (keep)** — prohibitions: refraining from work (melachah), so that nothing of the weekday disturbs the holiness of the day.

blocks.text: From the fact that the two words were spoken together, the Talmud also derives an important law: women, who are obligated to keep the prohibitions of Shabbat (“keep”), are equally obligated in the active commandments (“remember”), including kiddush (Berachot 20b). This is an exception to the general rule by which women are exempt from many commandments that are bound to time.

blocks.he: זָכוֹר וְשָׁמוֹר
blocks.text: “Remember” and “keep” are the two words of the commandment of Shabbat (Shemot 20:8 and Devarim 5:12): the active sanctification of the day, and refraining from work.
The sign of an everlasting covenant

blocks.he: וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת, לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת לְדֹרֹתָם בְּרִית עוֹלָם. בֵּינִי וּבֵין בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹת הִיא לְעֹלָם
blocks.translit: Veshamru bnei Yisrael et haShabbat, la'asot et haShabbat ledorotam brit olam. Beini uvein bnei Yisrael ot hi le'olam
blocks.ru: And let the children of Israel keep Shabbat, to observe Shabbat throughout their generations as an everlasting covenant. Between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign forever

blocks.text: The Torah calls Shabbat a **sign** (ot) and a **covenant** (brit) between the Almighty and the people of Israel. The Torah also applies the word “ot” to circumcision: it is an outward, visible mark of an inner bond. Neighbors and colleagues may never see how you pray, but they will notice that on Friday evening you are unavailable. These verses (“Veshamru”) are sung in the Friday evening prayer (according to Ashkenazi custom) and in the Shabbat morning kiddush.

In halacha Shabbat carries special weight. The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch (72:1) explains that Shabbat is a sign that the Almighty created the world in six days, and therefore keeping Shabbat is equivalent to testimony of faith in the Creator; and one who publicly violates Shabbat is, in many respects, equated by halacha with one who denies the entire Torah. For an Orthodox beit din, full observance of Shabbat is one of the required conditions of giyur.
More than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews.
blocks.ref: Ahad Ha'am (Asher Ginsberg), essay on Shabbat (1898)

blocks.text: Menuchah: a rest that one creates

Rest on Shabbat is not simply idleness or sleep. In Hebrew it is called **menuchah** — rest, peace, harmony. It is a time when you produce nothing and change nothing in the world, but simply live in it: you pray, eat with your family, talk, go for a walk, read, study Torah. The prophet Yeshayahu adds two further ideas — joy and honor:

blocks.he: וְקָרָאתָ לַשַּׁבָּת עֹנֶג, לִקְדוֹשׁ ה׳ מְכֻבָּד
blocks.translit: Vekarata laShabbat oneg, likdosh Adonai mechubad
blocks.ru: And you shall call Shabbat a delight, the holy day of the L-rd — honored

items: **Kavod Shabbat** (honoring Shabbat) — preparation: cleaning the home, washing, festive clothing, a set table.

**Oneg Shabbat** (delight in Shabbat) — tasty food, wine, songs, sleep, company; on Shabbat one does not fast (except for Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat) and one tries not to speak of sad things or of business.

blocks.he: מְנוּחָה
blocks.text: Shabbat rest: not only a rest from labor, but a state of inner peace and harmony with the Creator, with people and with the world.

It is important to understand that the “work” forbidden on Shabbat (melachah) is not the same thing as physical exertion. The Torah uses a special word, **melachah**, which refers to creative, transformative activity — the kind by which a person has mastery over nature. Moving a heavy sofa in your own apartment is not a melachah, but writing two letters is. This is set out in detail in the lesson on the 39 categories of work. The meaning, though, is simple: for six days a person is master of the world and changes it, and on the seventh acknowledges that the world does not belong to him.

At the beit din you are often asked: “Why do you keep Shabbat?” A good answer names both meanings from the Torah — the remembrance of Creation (Shemot 20) and the remembrance of the Exodus and of freedom (Devarim 5) — and adds something personal: what Shabbat in particular has changed in your life.

cards.back: In the Friday evening prayer (according to Ashkenazi custom) and in the Shabbat morning kiddush.

cards.back: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 27a; this idea entered the hymn “Lecha Dodi.”

lessons.title: Preparing for Shabbat and welcoming it: candles and Kabbalat Shabbat
keyIdeas: Preparation for Shabbat is part of kavod Shabbat: food, the home, clothing and tasks are prepared in advance, on Friday.
The candles are lit before sunset, by custom 18 minutes before; tosefet Shabbat is an “addition” to Shabbat.
At least two candles are lit — in memory of the words “remember” and “keep”; usually the woman of the house lights the candles.
Ashkenazim light the candles and then bless them, with their eyes covered; many Sephardim recite the blessing before lighting.
Kabbalat Shabbat is a service of psalms and “Lecha Dodi,” which took shape among the kabbalists of Tzfat in the 16th century; Shabbat is welcomed as a bride.

blocks.text: Shabbat begins on Friday morning

Shabbat cannot be “turned on” at the last minute: it is prepared in advance, and the preparation itself is part of the commandment of honoring Shabbat (kavod Shabbat). The sages said: “One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat” (Avodah Zarah 3a). The Talmud relates that great scholars prepared for Shabbat with their own hands: one cut vegetables, others chopped wood or lit the stove, and still others carried the purchases home (Shabbat 119a). No position exempts a person from serving Shabbat personally.

items: **Food** is prepared in advance: everything that needs to be cooked is cooked before Shabbat. Traditionally one prepares challot, wine or grape juice for kiddush, fish, a meat dish and a hot dish for the Shabbat lunch (among Ashkenazim — cholent, among Sephardim — chamin or dafina).
**The home** is cleaned and the table is set: a white tablecloth, the best dishes, candlesticks, a cup for kiddush, two challot under a cloth.
**Body and clothing**: it is customary to take a shower or a bath, to trim one's nails, and to put on festive clothing that differs from weekday clothes.
**Tasks**: pay bills in advance, finish correspondence, tell colleagues and friends that you will be unavailable, and set the phone aside.
**Tzedakah**: in many families, before the candles are lit, coins are put into a box for donations.

blocks.text: The time of entry: sunset

Shabbat begins at **sunset** (shkiah) on Friday. The time changes every week and depends on the place, so you use a Jewish calendar or a reliable website that gives the candle-lighting time for your city. By widespread custom the candles are lit **18 minutes before sunset**; in Jerusalem it is customary to light them 40 minutes before, and in some communities 20 or 30 minutes before. These minutes are a margin, so as to be sure not to be late.

In halacha there is the concept of **tosefet Shabbat** — “an addition to Shabbat”: the commandment to begin Shabbat a little before sunset and to end it a little after the stars appear. The time between sunset and the appearance of the stars is called **bein hashmashot** (twilight); it is treated stringently, as a time when Shabbat may already have begun. Shabbat may also be accepted earlier, starting from what is called plag haminchah (about an hour and a quarter of “seasonal” hours before sunset); one who has accepted Shabbat is already obligated to observe all its prohibitions. A woman, as a rule, accepts Shabbat by lighting the candles, and therefore after lighting she no longer does melachah.
Candle lighting

Lighting the Shabbat candles (Heb. **hadlakat nerot**) is the main rite of entering Shabbat. The Talmud connects it with the idea of **shalom bayit** — “peace in the home”: in a lit home people do not stumble and do not quarrel, and the Shabbat meal takes place in joy (Shabbat 23b). At least **two candles** are lit — in memory of the two words of the commandment, “remember” and “keep.” Many families light more: for example, by custom a candle is added for each child.

The commandment rests on every household. Traditionally it is fulfilled by the woman of the house — the Mishnah (Shabbat 2:6) mentions lighting a candle among three commandments especially connected with women. If there is no woman in the home, a man lights the candles; a person living alone — a man or a woman — lights the candles himself or herself. In many communities, girls light their own small candle from early childhood.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לְהַדְלִיק נֵר שֶׁל שַׁבָּת
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu lehadlik ner shel Shabbat
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the Shabbat candle

blocks.text: In Chabad and in some Sephardi communities one says “ner shel Shabbat kodesh” — “the candle of the holy Shabbat.” Both forms are correct: follow the custom of your community.

Usually one first says the blessing over every commandment and then performs it. But with the candles there is a difficulty: if the blessing is said first, then, in the view of many halachic authorities, you have already accepted Shabbat and may no longer kindle a fire. Therefore among **Ashkenazim** the order is as follows: first the candles are lit, then the eyes are covered with the palms, the blessing is said, and only then are the eyes opened and one looks at the flame — so that the enjoyment of the light comes only after the blessing. Many **Sephardim**, following the Shulchan Aruch, say the blessing before lighting.

After the blessing there is a beautiful custom: to stand for a few minutes before the candles and to pray in one's own words — for the family, the children, health. Many consider this moment especially favorable for personal prayer.

Halachic details (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 75): the candles are placed where people eat, so that the meal takes place by their light; on Shabbat they may not be moved (a candlestick with a flame is muktzeh); the candles should be long enough to burn at least until the end of dinner. If the sun has already set, one may not light them — a violation of Shabbat does not make up for a missed commandment.

blocks.he: שְׁלוֹם בַּיִת
blocks.text: “Peace in the home” — harmony in the family; according to the Talmud (Shabbat 23b), the main purpose of the Shabbat candles.
Kabbalat Shabbat — welcoming the Queen

The Talmud relates: on the eve of Shabbat Rabbi Chanina would dress in his finest clothes and say: “Come, let us go and welcome Shabbat the Queen,” and Rabbi Yannai would say: “Come, O bride! Come, O bride!” (Shabbat 119a). From these images, in the 16th century, the kabbalists of Tzfat created a special service — **Kabbalat Shabbat** (“the welcoming of Shabbat”). At first they would go out to welcome Shabbat in the fields, at sunset; later the service moved into the synagogue. Today it is read before the evening prayer (Maariv) on Friday in almost all communities.

items: Six psalms — Tehillim 95, 96, 97, 98, 99 and 29 — one for each weekday (so in the Ashkenazi rite; among Sephardim the selection and the order are partly different).
In many communities — the hymn “Ana BeKoach.”
The hymn “Lecha Dodi.”
Psalm 92, “Mizmor shir leyom haShabbat” — “A psalm, a song for the Shabbat day” — and Psalm 93.
Then the evening prayer, Maariv; on Shabbat the Amidah consists of seven blessings and includes “Vayechulu.”

blocks.text: The hymn **“Lecha Dodi”** (“Come, my beloved”) was written by the kabbalist Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz in Tzfat in the 16th century. The first letters of the eight stanzas spell the author's name — “Shlomo HaLevi.” In the hymn the groom is the people of Israel, and the bride is Shabbat. During the last stanza, “Bo'i veshalom” (“Come in peace”), the worshippers stand, turn toward the entrance of the synagogue, as if welcoming the bride as she enters, and bow.

blocks.he: לְכָה דוֹדִי לִקְרַאת כַּלָּה, פְּנֵי שַׁבָּת נְקַבְּלָה
blocks.translit: Lecha dodi likrat kallah, penei Shabbat nekabelah
blocks.ru: Come, my friend, to meet the bride; let us welcome the face of Shabbat
blocks.ref: Siddur, Kabbalat Shabbat (the refrain of “Lecha Dodi”)

blocks.he: שָׁמוֹר וְזָכוֹר בְּדִבּוּר אֶחָד, הִשְׁמִיעָנוּ אֵל הַמְיֻחָד
blocks.translit: Shamor vezachor bedibur echad, hishmi'anu El hameyuchad
blocks.ru: “Keep” and “remember” — in a single utterance the One G-d caused us to hear them

blocks.he: קַבָּלַת שַׁבָּת
blocks.text: “The welcoming of Shabbat” — a service of psalms and the hymn “Lecha Dodi” on Friday evening before Maariv; it took shape among the kabbalists of Tzfat in the 16th century.

After the prayer, people wish one another **“Shabbat shalom!”** (“a peaceful Shabbat”), and in Ashkenazi communities they often say in Yiddish “Gut Shabbes!” (“a good Shabbat”). Then everyone goes home to the festive meal — the next lesson is about it.

differs.text: In Reform communities the Friday evening service is often the main service of the week; the candles are frequently lit in the synagogue at the start of the service or at home at the start of dinner, even if this is already after sunset. Men and women take on all roles equally, and the service is often accompanied by music.

blocks.text: If you are just starting out: choose one Friday, find out the candle-lighting time for your city in advance, buy two candles and learn the blessing. Then go to Kabbalat Shabbat at a synagogue — even without knowing Hebrew, the melody of “Lecha Dodi” will quickly become your own.

cards.front: What did the sages say about preparing for Shabbat (Avodah Zarah 3a)?
cards.back: “One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat.”

cards.front: What is kavod Shabbat in practice?
cards.back: Honoring Shabbat: cleaning, bathing, festive clothing, a set table, and food prepared in advance.

cards.front: What is the hot Shabbat dish called among Ashkenazim and among Sephardim?
cards.back: Among Ashkenazim — cholent; among Sephardim — chamin (or dafina).

cards.front: According to the widespread custom, how many minutes before sunset are the candles lit?
cards.back: 18 minutes; in Jerusalem — 40 minutes; in some communities — 20–30.

cards.front: What is the minimum number of candles lit, and why?
cards.back: Two — in memory of the words “remember” and “keep.”

cards.front: With what concept does the Talmud connect the Shabbat candles (Shabbat 23b)?
cards.back: Shalom bayit — peace in the home.

cards.front: Who lights the candles if there is no woman in the household?
cards.back: A man; a person living alone lights them themselves.

cards.front: How does the blessing over the candles end?
cards.back: “…lehadlik ner shel Shabbat” — “to light the Shabbat candle.”

cards.front: Why do Ashkenazim cover their eyes during the blessing over the candles?
cards.back: The blessing marks the acceptance of Shabbat, so the candles are lit first, then the blessing is said with eyes covered, and only afterward does one look at the flames.

cards.front: What is tosefet Shabbat?
cards.back: “Adding to Shabbat” — beginning Shabbat a little before sunset and ending it a little after the stars come out.

cards.front: May the candles be lit if the sun has already set?
cards.back: According to halacha, no: after sunset, kindling a fire is a desecration of Shabbat.

cards.front: Where and when did the Kabbalat Shabbat service take shape?
cards.back: In Tzfat, in the 16th century, among the kabbalists.

cards.front: Which psalms are read at Kabbalat Shabbat (Ashkenazi rite)?
cards.back: Tehillim 95–99 and 29 — six psalms for the six weekdays, followed by 92 and 93.

cards.front: Who wrote “Lecha Dodi”?
cards.back: Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz, Tzfat, 16th century; his name is encoded in the first letters of the stanzas.

cards.front: What is done during the last stanza of “Lecha Dodi”?
cards.back: Everyone stands, turns toward the entrance and bows, welcoming the Shabbat bride.

cards.front: How is the refrain “Lecha dodi likrat kallah” translated?
cards.back: “Come, my beloved, to greet the bride; let us welcome the presence of Shabbat.”

cards.front: What is the Hebrew word for the sunset with which Shabbat begins?
cards.back: Shkiah.

cards.front: What is bein hashmashot?
cards.back: The twilight between sunset and the appearance of the stars; it is treated stringently, as a time when Shabbat may already have begun.

cards.front: From what time may Shabbat be accepted early?
cards.back: From plag haminchah — about an hour and a quarter of “seasonal” hours before sunset; one who has accepted Shabbat already observes all its prohibitions.

cards.front: Where are the Shabbat candles placed?
cards.back: Where the meal is eaten, so that the meal takes place by their light; on Shabbat they are not moved (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 75).

cards.front: How is the blessing over the candles said in Chabad and some Sephardi communities?
cards.back: “…ner shel Shabbat kodesh” — “the candle of the holy Shabbat.” Both forms are correct.

cards.front: Which words of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yannai became the basis of Kabbalat Shabbat?
cards.back: Rabbi Chanina: “Come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen”; Rabbi Yannai: “Come, O bride!” (Shabbat 119a).

cards.front: What tzedakah custom is connected with the candles?
cards.back: In many families, coins are put into a tzedakah box before the candles are lit.

cards.front: How do people greet one another after the Friday prayers?
cards.back: “Shabbat shalom!” — “a peaceful Shabbat”; Ashkenazim also say in Yiddish “Gut Shabbes!”

lessons.title: The Shabbat Meal: Kiddush, Challah and Zemirot
keyIdeas: The Friday night dinner follows a set order: “Shalom Aleichem,” “Eshet Chayil,” blessing the children, kiddush, netilat yadayim, “Hamotzi,” zemirot, Birkat Hamazon.
Kiddush fulfills “remember the Shabbat day”: it is said over wine or grape juice; one person says it on behalf of everyone, and women are obligated and may say it too.
Two challot (lechem mishneh) recall the double portion of manna on Friday; the challot are covered with a cloth and sprinkled with salt.
There are three meals on Shabbat: in the evening, during the day, and seudah shlishit toward evening — the word “today” is said three times in the account of the manna.
At the table people sing zemirot and share words of Torah; the meal ends with Birkat Hamazon with the special Shabbat insertion “Retzeh.”

blocks.text: The Table as a Small Temple

The Friday night dinner is the center of Shabbat at home. Tradition sees the dining table as resembling the altar in the Temple: candles burn on it, and bread, salt and wine are placed on it. The meal consists of several rituals that follow a set order. Once you have learned this order, you will be able to lead a Shabbat dinner yourself or take part in one confidently as a guest.

items: The song “Shalom Aleichem” — a greeting to the angels.
“Eshet Chayil” — “A Woman of Valor” (Mishlei (Proverbs) 31:10–31), according to the custom of many communities.
Blessing the children.
Kiddush over wine.
Washing the hands (netilat yadayim).
The “Hamotzi” blessing over two challot.
The meal with zemirot (Shabbat songs) and words of Torah.
The blessing after the meal (Birkat Hamazon).

blocks.text: “Shalom Aleichem” and Blessing the Children

The Talmud relates that on Friday evening two angels — a good one and an evil one — accompany a person home from the synagogue. If the candles are burning at home, the table is set and the beds are made, the good angel says: “May it be so next Shabbat as well,” and the evil angel is compelled to answer “amen” (Shabbat 119b). Hence the song “Shalom aleichem, malachei hasharet” — “Peace be upon you, ministering angels,” which is sung on returning from the synagogue.

blocks.he: שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת, מַלְאֲכֵי עֶלְיוֹן
blocks.translit: Shalom aleichem, malachei hasharet, malachei Elyon
blocks.ru: Peace be upon you, ministering angels, angels of the Most High

blocks.text: Then the parents bless the children, placing their hands on the children's heads. Sons are blessed with the words of Yaakov: “May G-d make you like Ephraim and Menashe” (Bereshit 48:20); daughters — “May G-d make you like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah.” After this the Priestly Blessing is recited (Bamidbar (Numbers) 6:24–26): “May the L-rd bless you and keep you…”

blocks.he: יְשִׂמְךָ אֱלֹהִים כְּאֶפְרַיִם וְכִמְנַשֶּׁה
blocks.translit: Yesimcha Elohim ke'Ephraim vechiMenashe
blocks.ru: May G-d make you like Ephraim and Menashe

blocks.text: Kiddush: Sanctifying the Day over Wine

**Kiddush** (“sanctification”) fulfills the commandment “Remember the Shabbat day to keep it holy.” The sages explained: “Remember it — over wine” (Pesachim 106a): Shabbat is sanctified with words while holding a cup of wine. Wine is a symbol of joy, and the festive words said over it turn an ordinary dinner into a holy meal. Kiddush may be said over grape juice: the same blessing is said over it. One person recites kiddush on behalf of everyone, and the listeners answer “amen” and thereby fulfill the commandment. Women are obligated in kiddush equally with men and may recite it on behalf of others.

Kiddush is said standing or sitting, according to the family's custom. It begins with the verses about the seventh day of creation (Bereshit 2:1–3); before them, the last words of the preceding verse — “yom hashishi” (“the sixth day”) — are said quietly, so that the first letters form the Name of the Almighty.

blocks.he: וַיְכֻלּוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ וְכָל צְבָאָם. וַיְכַל אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי מְלַאכְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה, וַיִּשְׁבֹּת בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי מִכָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
blocks.translit: Vayechulu hashamayim veha'aretz vechol tzeva'am. Vayechal Elohim bayom hashevi'i melachto asher asah, vayishbot bayom hashevi'i mikol melachto asher asah
blocks.ru: The heavens and the earth and all their host were completed. And by the seventh day G-d completed His work which He had done, and He ceased on the seventh day from all His work which He had done

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגָּפֶן
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, borei pri hagafen
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine

blocks.text: Then comes the blessing of the sanctification of the day itself. In it both meanings of Shabbat from the first lesson are heard: Shabbat was given “in remembrance of the work of creation” (zikaron lema'aseh bereshit) and “in remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt” (zecher litziat Mitzrayim). Kiddush ends with the words:

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳, מְקַדֵּשׁ הַשַּׁבָּת
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, mekadesh haShabbat
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, who sanctifies Shabbat

blocks.text: The person who recited kiddush drinks from the wine, and then the wine is shared with everyone sitting at the table. On Shabbat morning, before the midday meal, kiddush is also made — it is shorter: usually the verses “Veshamru” (Shemot 31:16–17) are read and the blessing over wine is said.

Halachic details (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 271; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 77): the cup must hold at least a **revi'it** — about 86 ml according to the calculation of Rav Chaim Naeh, or about 150 ml according to the Chazon Ish; the one reciting drinks at least a “cheekful” (the greater part of a revi'it). Kiddush is valid only “in the place of the meal” (kiddush bimkom seudah): one eats right after it. Before kiddush on Shabbat one may not eat or drink. If there is no wine, the evening kiddush is said over the two challot; the morning kiddush, according to Ashkenazi custom, may also be made over another significant beverage (chamar medinah).

blocks.he: קִדּוּשׁ
blocks.text: “Sanctification” — the blessing over wine at the beginning of the Shabbat (and festival) meal, by which the commandment “remember the Shabbat day” is fulfilled.
Washing the Hands and the Two Challot

Before eating bread, a ritual **washing of the hands** (netilat yadayim) is performed: a special cup (natlah) is filled with water and poured over each hand — among Ashkenazim usually twice, in the Chabad tradition and among many Sephardim three times, starting with the right. Then, raising the hands, one says the blessing and dries them. It is customary not to speak between the washing and the blessing over bread. In most communities the washing is done after kiddush, and in some (for example, among German Jews) before it.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל נְטִילַת יָדָיִם
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu al netilat yadayim
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the washing of the hands

differs.text: In Reform practice, the ritual washing of the hands before bread is usually not considered obligatory and is not performed in many families; the candles, kiddush and the blessing over bread remain central.

blocks.text: On the table lie **two whole challot** — **lechem mishneh** (“double bread”). This recalls the manna in the wilderness: on weekdays each person gathered one portion, but on Friday the manna fell in a double amount, and on Shabbat it was not gathered (Shemot 16:22–29). The challot are covered with a beautiful cloth — according to one explanation, just as the manna lay between two layers of dew; according to another, so that the bread does not “see” that the blessing over the wine preceded it. The person making the blessing takes both challot, says “Hamotzi,” cuts one, sprinkles it with salt (as the offerings in the Temple were salted) and gives a piece to everyone.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth

blocks.he: חַלָּה
blocks.text: Originally, the portion of dough that was separated for the kohen (Bamidbar 15:20); today the braided Shabbat bread is also called by this name. The two challot on the table are the lechem mishneh.
Three Meals, Zemirot and the Blessing after the Meal

On Shabbat one is to eat **three meals**: on Friday evening, on Shabbat during the day after the morning prayers, and a third toward Shabbat evening (seudah shlishit). The Talmud derives this from the fact that in the account of the manna the word “today” is said of Shabbat three times (Shemot 16:25; Shabbat 117b). Each meal begins with bread — two challot.

Between courses people sing **zemirot** — Shabbat songs. Many of them were written by poets of the Middle Ages and the early modern period: for example, the Aramaic hymn “Yah Ribon Olam” (“Master of the World”) was composed by Rabbi Yisrael Najara in the 16th century. People also sing “Menuchah VeSimchah,” “Yom Zeh Mechubad,” “Tzur Mishelo” and others. It is customary at the table to share something from the weekly Torah portion — so the meal also becomes a lesson.

The meal ends with the **blessing after the meal** (Birkat Hamazon). On Shabbat, Psalm 126, “Shir Hama'alot” (“When the L-rd brings back the captives of Zion…”), is sung before it, and a special insertion, “Retzeh” — a request for Shabbat rest — is added to the text of the blessing itself.

If you are invited to a Shabbat dinner with a religious family, don't hesitate to ask your hosts about the order: they will gladly explain everything. Answer “amen” to kiddush, do not talk between washing your hands and the blessing over bread, and do not use your phone at the table.

cards.front: To whom is the song “Shalom Aleichem” addressed?
cards.back: To the ministering angels who, according to the Talmud (Shabbat 119b), accompany a person home from the synagogue.

cards.front: With what verse are sons blessed on Friday evening?
cards.back: “May G-d make you like Ephraim and Menashe” (Bereshit 48:20).

cards.front: How are daughters blessed?
cards.back: “May G-d make you like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah.”

cards.front: What is kiddush?
cards.back: The sanctification of Shabbat with words over a cup of wine at the beginning of the meal.

cards.front: How do we know that kiddush is made over wine?
cards.back: The sages: “Remember it — over wine” (Pesachim 106a).

cards.front: With which verses does the evening kiddush begin?
cards.back: With “Vayechulu” — Bereshit 2:1–3, about the completion of creation.

cards.front: What blessing is said over wine?
cards.back: "…borei pri ha-gafen" — "who creates the fruit of the vine."

cards.front: With what words does kiddush end?
cards.back: “Baruch atah Adonai, mekadesh haShabbat” — “who sanctifies Shabbat.”

cards.front: What two meanings of Shabbat are mentioned in kiddush?
cards.back: Remembrance of the work of creation and remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt.

cards.front: What is the minimum volume of a kiddush cup?
cards.back: A revi'it: about 86 ml (Rav Ch. Naeh) or about 150 ml (Chazon Ish).

cards.front: What is “kiddush bimkom seudah”?
cards.back: The rule that kiddush is valid only where a meal is eaten right after it.

cards.front: What blessing accompanies the washing of the hands?
cards.back: “…al netilat yadayim” — “commanded us concerning the washing of the hands.”

cards.front: What is lechem mishneh, and what does it commemorate?
cards.back: Two whole challot — in memory of the double portion of manna on Friday (Shemot 16:22).

cards.front: What blessing is said over bread?
cards.back: “…hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz” — “who brings forth bread from the earth.”

cards.front: How many meals are required on Shabbat, and from where is this derived?
cards.back: Three: “today” is said of Shabbat three times in Shemot 16:25 (Shabbat 117b).

cards.front: What are zemirot?
cards.back: Shabbat songs sung at the table, for example “Yah Ribon Olam” by R. Yisrael Najara (16th c.).

cards.front: What is added to Birkat Hamazon on Shabbat?
cards.back: Psalm 126, “Shir Hama'alot,” is sung before it, and the insertion “Retzeh” is added to the text.

cards.front: To what does tradition compare the Shabbat table?
cards.back: To the altar in the Temple: on it are candles, bread, salt and wine.

cards.front: Why are the challot covered with a cloth?
cards.back: Just as the manna lay between two layers of dew; or so that the bread does not “see” that the wine preceded it in the blessing.

cards.front: Why is the challah sprinkled with salt?
cards.back: Just as the offerings in the Temple were salted.

cards.front: How does the morning kiddush differ from the evening one?
cards.back: It is shorter: usually “Veshamru” (Shemot 31:16–17) is read and the blessing over wine is said.

cards.front: Over what is the evening kiddush said if there is neither wine nor grape juice?
cards.back: Over the two challot. The morning kiddush, according to Ashkenazi custom, may be made over a significant beverage (chamar medinah).

cards.front: How many times is water poured over each hand during netilat yadayim?
cards.back: Among Ashkenazim usually twice; in Chabad and among many Sephardim — three times, starting with the right.

cards.front: What did the word “challah” originally mean?
cards.back: The portion of dough that was separated for the kohen (Bamidbar 15:20).

cards.front: Why is “yom hashishi” said quietly before “Vayechulu”?
cards.back: So that the first letters of “yom hashishi” and of the opening of “Vayechulu” form the Name of the Almighty.

lessons.title: The 39 Categories of Work, Muktzeh, Eruv and Pikuach Nefesh
keyIdeas: The 39 primary categories of work (avot melachot) were derived by the sages from the work involved in building the Mishkan.
Melachah is a conscious, purposeful, creative act that changes the world; the amount of effort involved does not matter.
Muktzeh are items that are not moved on Shabbat without need (money, tools, valuable objects), so as not to come to perform melachah.
An eruv, through a symbolic enclosure and shared food, unites separate domains and permits carrying within it; it is checked every week.
To save a life (pikuach nefesh), Shabbat must be set aside; in a case of doubt one acts just as in the case of a clear danger.

blocks.text: How We Know What “Work” Is

This lesson examines in detail the classical system of the 39 melachot — the language in which Jewish tradition speaks about Shabbat. It is worth knowing in every movement: both for those who accept these laws as binding and for those who build the holiness of the day in other ways. The Reform and Conservative approaches are set out at the end of the lesson with the same thoroughness, not as a brief side note.

The Torah repeatedly forbids “all work” (kol melachah) on Shabbat, but nowhere does it explicitly list what this concept includes. The sages found the key in the juxtaposition of two topics. In the book of Shemot, the command to build the **Mishkan** (the portable sanctuary in the wilderness) appears twice alongside the commandment of Shabbat (Shemot 31:12–17 and 35:1–3). From this they concluded: even for the sake of building the sanctuary one may not violate Shabbat, and therefore the forbidden “work” is precisely those types of activity that were needed to make the Mishkan (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 49b).

The Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2) lists **39 primary categories of work** — “avot melachot” (“fathers of labors”; literally: “forty less one”). These are agriculture and baking bread (for the showbread), making fabrics and leather (for the curtains and coverings of the Mishkan), writing (marks were made on the boards of the Mishkan), building, work with fire, and carrying. The general principle: **melachah** is a conscious, purposeful, creative act by which a person changes the world. How strenuous the work is does not matter.

blocks.he: לֹא תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ בְּכֹל מֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
blocks.translit: Lo teva'aru esh bechol moshvoteichem beyom haShabbat
blocks.ru: You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the Shabbat day

blocks.he: מְלָאכָה
blocks.text: Creative work forbidden on Shabbat; the 39 primary categories (avot melachot) are derived from the work involved in building the Mishkan.
The 39 Melachot by Group

items: **Bread (from field to oven), 11:** sowing (zore'a), plowing (choresh), reaping (kotzer), gathering sheaves (me'amer), threshing (dash), winnowing (zoreh), selecting (borer), grinding (tochen), sifting (meraked), kneading (lash), baking (ofeh; this also includes cooking — bishul).

**Fabric (from wool to garment), 13:** shearing wool (gozez), whitening/laundering (melaben), combing (menapetz), dyeing (tzove'a), spinning (toveh), stretching the warp (meisech), making two heddle loops (oseh shtei batei nirin), weaving two threads (oreg), separating two threads (potze'a), tying a knot (kosher), untying a knot (matir), sewing two stitches (tofer), tearing in order to sew two stitches (kore'a).
**Leather, 7:** trapping an animal (tzad), slaughtering (shochet), skinning (mafshit), salting/curing (molei'ach), tanning (me'abed), scraping (memachek), cutting to shape (mechatech).
**Writing, 2:** writing two letters (kotev), erasing in order to write two letters (mochek).
**Building, 2:** building (boneh), demolishing (soter).
**Fire, 2:** extinguishing (mechabeh), kindling (mav'ir).
**Completion, 1:** “the final hammer blow” (makeh bapatish) — bringing any object to its finished state.
**Carrying, 1:** carrying from one domain to another (motzi mereshut lereshut).

blocks.text: Each primary melachah has **derivatives** (toladot) — actions of the same nature and purpose. For example, squeezing juice from fruit is a derivative of “threshing” (separating the contents from the shell), and boiling water is a derivative of “baking/cooking.” In addition, the sages established protective prohibitions (shevut): for example, not discussing weekday matters and business deals, not trading, and not asking a non-Jew to perform melachah for you. The prohibition of “selecting” (borer) means in practice that from a mixture one takes what one wants rather than picking out what one doesn't want, by hand, and for immediate use.
Muktzeh: what is “set aside”

**Muktzeh** (Heb. “set aside”) refers to objects that the Sages prohibited moving on Shabbat, so that a person would not come to do melachah and so that the day would not resemble a weekday (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 308–310). The main categories are: things not meant for any use at all, such as stones, branches and money; tools for forbidden work, such as a hammer, a pen, scissors or a phone (these may be moved if the item is needed for a permitted purpose or if its place needs to be cleared); valuable items that people treasure and never use for anything other than their purpose; and a base for a forbidden object, for example a candlestick holding burning candles. Food, dishes, books and clothing are not muktzeh.
Carrying and the eruv

Halacha distinguishes between “domains”: the private domain (reshut hayachid), for example an enclosed house and yard; the public domain (reshut harabim), a major street; and an intermediate domain (karmelit). On Shabbat one may not carry objects from a private domain into a public one or vice versa, nor carry them a distance of four cubits within a public domain. This applies to keys, a handkerchief in your pocket, a bag with a tallit, or a baby stroller. An **eruv** (“mixing”) is a halachic merging of territory: a neighborhood or city is surrounded by a symbolic enclosure of poles and wire (tzurat hapetach, “the form of a doorway”), and the residents merge their domains through shared food (eruv chatzerot). Within a valid eruv, carrying is permitted. The eruv is checked every week, and the community announces whether it is in order. There are other kinds of eruv as well: eruv techumin (extending the permitted walking distance beyond the city, 2,000 cubits) and eruv tavshilin (for cooking food for Shabbat on a festival).

blocks.he: עֵרוּב
blocks.text: A halachic “merging” of domains by a symbolic enclosure, which allows objects to be carried within it on Shabbat.
Electricity

There was no electricity in the era of the Mishnah, so the halachic authorities of the 20th century applied general principles to it. The accepted Orthodox position is that turning electrical appliances on and off on Shabbat is **forbidden**. An incandescent bulb is a glowing filament, that is, real fire (kindling and, in the view of many, “cooking” the metal). Opinions differ about closing a circuit as such: some see it as “building” or “completing” (the position of the Chazon Ish), others as a rabbinic prohibition. In practice this means: do not use lights, the phone, the computer or the stove; do not open the refrigerator if a light turns on when you do (people unscrew the bulb in advance). For convenience people use **Shabbat timers** set before Shabbat, an electric hot plate (plata) for warming food cooked in advance, and in high-rise buildings and hotels in Israel a “Shabbat elevator” that runs on its own, stopping at every floor (its permissibility is also debated).

differs.text: In 1950 the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly (CJLS) permitted the use of electric light on Shabbat, understanding switching on a lamp differently from kindling a fire. At the same time, the movement urges people to avoid using devices that turn Shabbat into a weekday (work, shopping, noisy entertainment); within Masorti, opinions on gadgets vary.

blocks.text: Pikuach nefesh: life comes before Shabbat

The most important rule about Shabbat: to save a life (**pikuach nefesh**), it is not merely permitted but **obligatory** to break Shabbat. The Torah says of the mitzvot: “…which a person shall do and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5), and the Sages add: “live by them, and not die because of them” (Yoma 85b). The same passage gives another reason as well: “Break one Shabbat for his sake, so that he may keep many Shabbatot.” The Shulchan Aruch rules that Shabbat is broken for a dangerously ill person, and that whoever hurries is praiseworthy, while whoever delays by asking questions sheds blood (Orach Chaim 328:2).

blocks.he: אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה אֹתָם הָאָדָם וָחַי בָּהֶם
blocks.translit: Asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam vachai bahem
blocks.ru: …which a person shall do and live by them

items: Calling an ambulance, taking a woman in labor to the hospital, giving necessary medicine when life is at risk: these are done immediately, without hesitation.
If it is unclear whether there is danger, act as if there is: even a doubt about a threat to life gives the right to break Shabbat.
Doctors, nurses and rescue workers work on Shabbat when it is needed to save lives.

blocks.text: The melachot seem complicated, but they are learned gradually, through practice. Don’t try to learn everything in a week: start with the essentials (don’t light a fire, don’t cook, don’t write, don’t use electronics or money) and work through the details with your rabbi or mentor.
The Reform view of the melachot and the holiness of the day

Reform (Progressive) Judaism does not regard the 39 melachot as a binding legal code. This is not because Shabbat is “less important” to it. On the contrary: Shabbat remains the heart of the Jewish week, a sign of the covenant and the day when a person stops being a slave to their affairs. The difference lies in **how** the holiness of the day is built. Classical Reform thought starts from the idea that the Torah was given within history and calls for a conscious, informed response from every Jew, rather than mechanical observance of all the protective fences of the Oral Law.

Therefore, in Reform practice, driving to the synagogue, electric light, cooking and using the phone are usually not considered in themselves a violation of Shabbat. What is more often seen as forbidden is whatever brings back weekday toil, commerce, rush and indifference: paid work, shopping, business correspondence, a bustle that leaves no room for prayer, family, study and rest. Many communities ask directly: come to the Friday service, light candles, make kiddush, sit down at the table without hurrying, switch off at least some of the weekday noise.

This is not “permission to do everything.” Informed choice assumes that a person **first studies** the melachot, the meaning of Shabbat and the practice of their community, and then builds their own honest pattern for the day. Some take on nearly complete traditional rest, some choose a few strict personal limits (for example, not working and not spending money, but driving to the synagogue), and some put the service, the meal and the family at the center. At a Reform beit din, what is expected is not a vow that “I don’t turn on the light,” but a clear account: what your Shabbat actually looks like, what you already keep, what you are working toward, and why it is holy to you.

In Reform communities, the Friday evening service is often the main service of the week: mixed seating, equal participation of men and women, frequently an organ or other instruments, reading in Hebrew and in a language people understand. Candles are sometimes lit in the synagogue at the start of the service even if the sun has already set, not out of carelessness, but because the community’s welcoming of Shabbat itself becomes the ritual. The home table is not abandoned: kiddush, challah and time with loved ones remain the pillars of the day.

Pikuach nefesh, saving a life, is just as unconditional in Reform Judaism as in the other movements: human life is more important than the rest of the day. The difference is not in the value of life, but in which everyday actions count as “work” at all.

The Conservative (Masorti) movement takes a middle position: Shabbat is binding, but a number of modern questions are resolved through responsa. Thus, in 1950 the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly (CJLS) permitted the use of electric light and, in a well-known ruling, driving to the synagogue if a person could not otherwise attend services. At the same time, work, commerce and turning the day into an ordinary weekday are still rejected. Here, as on the Reform path, it is important to speak the language of your own community, not presenting others’ norms as your own and not calling another path “not real.”

cards.front: How did the Sages determine which kinds of work are forbidden on Shabbat?
cards.back: From the juxtaposition in the Torah of the mitzvah of Shabbat with the building of the Mishkan (Shemot 31; 35): the kinds of work needed for the Mishkan are forbidden.

cards.front: How many main categories of work does the Mishnah list, and where?
cards.back: 39 (avot melachot): Mishnah Shabbat 7:2.

cards.front: What defines a melachah: effort or result?
cards.back: The creative, purposeful nature of the action; how strenuous the work is makes no difference.

cards.front: What groups make up the 39 melachot?
cards.back: Bread (11), cloth (13), leather (7), writing (2), building (2), fire (2), completion (1), carrying (1).

cards.front: Which melachah does cooking food fall under?
cards.back: Under “ofeh,” baking (bishul, cooking).

cards.front: What are toladot?
cards.back: Derivative melachot: actions with the same nature and purpose as the main melachah.

cards.front: What is makeh bepatish?
cards.back: “The final hammer blow”: bringing an object to completion; one of the 39 melachot.

cards.front: How do you “select” correctly on Shabbat without violating the prohibition of borer?
cards.back: Take what you want from what you don’t, by hand, and for immediate use.

cards.front: What is muktzeh? Give examples.
cards.back: Objects that may not be moved on Shabbat: money, stones, a phone, a hammer, a candlestick with a flame.

cards.front: What is eruv chatzerot?
cards.back: The merging of domains through a symbolic enclosure and shared food, which permits carrying objects inside it.

cards.front: What may you not do on Shabbat without an eruv?
cards.back: Carry things from the house into the street and along the street: keys, bags, a stroller.

cards.front: What is the general Orthodox approach to electricity on Shabbat?
cards.back: Turning appliances on and off is forbidden; people use timers set in advance and a hot plate (plata).

cards.front: What did the Conservative movement’s CJLS permit regarding electricity in 1950?
cards.back: Using electric light on Shabbat.

cards.front: What is pikuach nefesh?
cards.back: Saving a life; for its sake, Shabbat must be broken.

cards.front: Which verse is the source of the principle of pikuach nefesh?
cards.back: “…and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5): “and not die because of them” (Yoma 85b).

cards.front: What do you do when in doubt whether there is a threat to life?
cards.back: The same as when there is a threat: Shabbat is broken; whoever hurries is praiseworthy (Orach Chaim 328:2).

cards.front: Which verse explicitly forbids fire on Shabbat?
cards.back: “You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the Shabbat day” (Shemot 35:3).

cards.front: What is shevut?
cards.back: Protective prohibitions of the Sages: not discussing weekday matters, not trading, not asking a non-Jew to perform a melachah.

cards.front: What three kinds of domain does halacha distinguish?
cards.back: Private (reshut hayachid), public (reshut harabim) and intermediate (karmelit).

cards.front: What is tzurat hapetach?
cards.back: “The form of a doorway”: the symbolic enclosure of an eruv, made of poles and wire.

cards.front: What are eruv techumin and eruv tavshilin?
cards.back: Techumin concerns the permitted distance beyond the city (2,000 cubits); tavshilin allows cooking food for Shabbat on a festival.

cards.front: Why, according to the Orthodox position, is an incandescent bulb treated as fire?
cards.back: Its glowing filament is real fire: this is kindling and, in the view of many, “cooking” the metal.

cards.front: What second reason for pikuach nefesh does Yoma 85b give?
cards.back: “Break one Shabbat for his sake, so that he may keep many Shabbatot.”

cards.front: What is a “Shabbat elevator”?
cards.back: An elevator that runs by itself on Shabbat and stops at every floor; its permissibility is debated.

lessons.title: Havdalah: bidding farewell to Shabbat
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Shabbat 29:1
keyIdeas: Havdalah means “separation”: the mitzvah is to sanctify Shabbat on its entry with kiddush and on its departure with havdalah (Rambam, Laws of Shabbat 29:1).
Shabbat ends when three medium-sized stars are visible, usually 40–50 minutes after sunset; many Chassidim and some communities wait 72 minutes.
Havdalah requires wine, spices and a candle with several wicks; the order of the blessings follows the acronym “Yavneh.”
The spices revive the soul as the “additional soul” (neshamah yeteirah) departs; fire was Adam’s first creation.
After havdalah people sing “Eliyahu HaNavi” and wish each other “Shavua tov”; many hold a melaveh malkah, “escorting the Queen.”

blocks.text: Sanctifying both the entry and the departure

Shabbat does not break off suddenly: just as it is welcomed with ceremony, so it is escorted out. The farewell ritual is called **havdalah**, “separation.” The Rambam explains that the mitzvah “Remember the Shabbat day to keep it holy” means sanctifying Shabbat with words at its entry, through kiddush, and at its departure, through havdalah (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Shabbat 29:1). Kiddush and havdalah are two frames of a single picture: the first separates the holy day from the weekdays at the beginning, the second at the end.

blocks.he: הַבְדָּלָה
blocks.text: “Separation”: a ritual over wine, spices and fire at the conclusion of Shabbat and festivals, separating holy time from ordinary time.
When Shabbat ends

Shabbat ends on Saturday evening, when **three medium-sized stars** are visible in the sky (tzeit hakochavim). Jewish calendars list this time for each city; it usually comes about 40–50 minutes after sunset, but different communities use different calculations, and many Chassidim and some other communities wait 72 minutes (the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam). This is why Shabbat lasts more than 24 hours, about 25 hours.

After the stars come out, the evening prayer (Maariv) for the departure of Shabbat is recited, in which a special prayer of separation, “Atah chonantanu,” is inserted into the fourth blessing of the Amidah. Someone who has prayed may already do melachah; someone who has not prayed but needs to work before havdalah says: “Baruch hamavdil bein kodesh lechol” (“Blessed is He who separates between holy and ordinary”). However, one may not eat or drink (except water) before havdalah over wine (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 299). If havdalah was not made on Saturday night, it can be made up until the end of Tuesday, but without the candle and spices.
Four blessings

Havdalah requires three items: **a cup of wine** (or grape juice), **spices** (besamim) and **a candle with several wicks**. The order of the blessings is remembered by the Hebrew acronym **יַבְנֶ״ה** (Yavneh): **y**ayin, wine; **b**esamim, spices; **n**er, candle; **h**avdalah, the blessing of separation. Before the blessings, in the Ashkenazi rite, verses of hope and salvation are recited, beginning with the words of the prophet Yeshayahu:

blocks.he: הִנֵּה אֵל יְשׁוּעָתִי, אֶבְטַח וְלֹא אֶפְחָד
blocks.translit: Hineh El yeshuati, evtach velo efchad
blocks.ru: Behold, G-d is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid

blocks.text: **1. Wine.** The cup is filled to the brim so that the wine spills over a little, as a sign of abundance and blessing for the whole week. The same blessing is said as in kiddush: “…borei pri hagafen.” The wine is drunk only after all the blessings.

**2. Spices.** The Sages teach that on Shabbat a person is given an “additional soul” (neshamah yeteirah), and at the conclusion of Shabbat it departs (Beitzah 16a). The fragrance of the spices “revives” the soul, which is saddened at parting from Shabbat. People use cloves, cinnamon, myrtle or a special spice box (among Ashkenazim it is often shaped like a little tower).

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי בְשָׂמִים
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, borei minei vesamim
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord our G-d, King of the universe, who creates various kinds of spices

blocks.text: Among Sephardim, the blessing often depends on the kind of spice: over fragrant trees and shrubs (for example, myrtle) one says “borei atzei vesamim,” over herbs “borei isvei vesamim”; Ashkenazim say “borei minei vesamim” over any spices.

**3. Fire.** The Talmud relates that at the conclusion of the first Shabbat in history the Almighty gave Adam understanding, and by rubbing two stones together he produced fire (Pesachim 54a). Fire is the first human creation and a symbol that it is now possible to create again. Because the blessing says “lights” in the plural, a braided candle with several wicks is used (or two candles held together). After the blessing, people bring their fingers close to the flame and look at the light reflected in their fingernails, in order to benefit from the light over which the blessing was said.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, בּוֹרֵא מְאוֹרֵי הָאֵשׁ
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, borei me'orei ha'esh
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord our G-d, King of the universe, who creates the lights of fire

blocks.text: **4. Separation.** The cup is raised again and the main blessing is said. It lists four separations established by the Creator:

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין קֹדֶשׁ לְחוֹל, בֵּין אוֹר לְחֹשֶׁךְ, בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים, בֵּין יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי לְשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳, הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין קֹדֶשׁ לְחוֹל
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, hamavdil bein kodesh lechol, bein or lechoshech, bein Yisrael la'amim, bein yom hashevi'i lesheshet yemei hama'aseh. Baruch atah Adonai, hamavdil bein kodesh lechol
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, Lord our G-d, King of the universe, who separates between holy and ordinary, between light and darkness, between Israel and the nations, between the seventh day and the six days of work. Blessed are You, Lord, who separates between holy and ordinary

blocks.text: Then the person who made havdalah drinks the wine while seated, and the candle is extinguished with a few drops of the spilled wine. Some moisten their eyelids with this wine or put drops in their pockets, for good fortune in the new week; these are folk customs, not obligations.

According to most halachic authorities, women are obligated in havdalah, as in kiddush, and they usually hear havdalah from their husband or another man; among Ashkenazim the custom is that women do not drink the wine from the havdalah cup. If a woman has no one to hear havdalah from, she makes it herself. If Shabbat leads directly into a festival, havdalah is included in the festival kiddush, and spices are not used.
After havdalah

After havdalah people sing the song “Eliyahu HaNavi” about the prophet Eliyahu, who, according to tradition, will come to announce the redemption, and wish each other **“Shavua tov!”**, “A good week!” (in Yiddish, “A gute vokh”). Many hold a **melaveh malkah** (“escorting the Queen”), a fourth, small meal on Saturday evening that tradition connects with King David. In this way Shabbat is escorted out with honor, like a dear guest seen to the door.
Eliyahu will yet come before the long-awaited Mashiach and prepare the hearts of the people (Malachi 3:23; Rambam, Laws of Kings 12:2).

Havdalah is a short, beautiful and very family-centered ritual, just a few minutes long. Children especially love holding the candle and smelling the spices. If you live alone, you can make havdalah yourself: all you need is a candle with several wicks, some cloves and a cup of juice or wine.

cards.front: What does the word “havdalah” mean?
cards.back: “Separation”: between holy Shabbat and the weekdays.

cards.front: According to the Rambam, from which mitzvah is havdalah derived?
cards.back: From “Remember the Shabbat day to keep it holy”: sanctifying it at its entry (kiddush) and at its departure (havdalah). Laws of Shabbat 29:1.

cards.front: When does Shabbat end?
cards.back: When three medium-sized stars appear (tzeit hakochavim); some wait 72 minutes after sunset.

cards.front: Roughly how long does Shabbat last?
cards.back: About 25 hours.

cards.front: What three items are needed for havdalah?
cards.back: A cup of wine (or juice), spices and a candle with several wicks.

cards.front: What is the acronym for the order of the havdalah blessings?
cards.back: יַבְנֶ״ה: yayin (wine), besamim (spices), ner (candle), havdalah.

cards.front: Why do people smell spices at the conclusion of Shabbat?
cards.back: The “additional soul” (neshamah yeteirah) departs, and the fragrance revives the soul (Beitzah 16a).

cards.front: What blessing do Ashkenazim say over spices?
cards.back: “…borei minei vesamim”: “who creates various kinds of spices.”

cards.front: Why does the havdalah candle have several wicks?
cards.back: The blessing “borei me'orei ha'esh” says “lights” in the plural.

cards.front: Why is fire blessed in havdalah?
cards.back: At the conclusion of the first Shabbat, Adam produced fire (Pesachim 54a); fire is a sign that it is possible to create again.

cards.front: Why do people look at their fingernails by the havdalah candle?
cards.back: To benefit from the light over which the blessing was said.

cards.front: What four separations are named in havdalah?
cards.back: Holy and ordinary, light and darkness, Israel and the nations, the seventh day and the six weekdays.

cards.front: What is inserted into the Amidah of the evening prayer at the conclusion of Shabbat?
cards.back: “Atah chonantanu”: a prayer of separation in the fourth blessing.

cards.front: May you eat before havdalah?
cards.back: No, you may not eat or drink (except water) before havdalah over wine.

cards.front: What do you say in order to do melachah before havdalah?
cards.back: “Baruch hamavdil bein kodesh lechol.”

cards.front: What is melaveh malkah?
cards.back: “Escorting the Queen” — a fourth meal on Saturday night, associated with King David.

cards.front: How do people greet each other after havdalah?
cards.back: “Shavua tov!” — “A good week!” (Yiddish: “A gute voch”).

cards.front: How is the havdalah candle put out?
cards.back: With a few drops of wine poured from the cup.

cards.front: Which blessings over spices do Sephardim often say?
cards.back: Over fragrant trees (myrtle) — “borei atzei vesamim”; over herbs — “borei isvei vesamim”.

cards.front: Until when can a missed havdalah be made up?
cards.back: Until the end of Tuesday, but without the candle and the spices.

cards.front: How is havdalah made when Shabbat goes straight into a festival?
cards.back: It is included in the festival kiddush, and spices are not used.

cards.front: Why is the havdalah cup filled to the brim?
cards.back: The wine overflows a little — as a sign of abundance and blessing for the whole week.

cards.front: With what words do the verses before havdalah begin (Ashkenazi rite)?
cards.back: “Hineh El yeshuati” — “Behold, G-d is my salvation” (Yeshayahu 12:2).

cards.front: What song is sung after havdalah?
cards.back: “Eliyahu HaNavi” — about the prophet who, according to tradition, will come to announce the redemption.

cards.front: Are women obligated in havdalah?
cards.back: According to most opinions — yes. Usually a woman listens to the havdalah of her husband or another man, and if there is no one to hear it from, she makes it herself. Among Ashkenazim, by custom, women do not drink the havdalah wine.

cards.front: When will the prophet Eliyahu come?
cards.back: Before Mashiach, who is still awaited. Eliyahu will prepare the hearts of the people (Malachi 3:23; Rambam, Laws of Kings 12:2).

lessons.title: Shabbat in the different movements and how to begin keeping it
citations: CCAR “A Statement of Principles for Reform Judaism” (Pittsburgh, 1999)
keyIdeas: All the movements see Shabbat as the center of Jewish life: candles, kiddush, challot, services and havdalah are found in every community.
Orthodoxy observes all 39 melachot and the rabbinic prohibitions; for its beit din, full observance of Shabbat is one of the key conditions for giyur.
The 1950 CJLS responsum permitted electric light and, where the distance is too far to walk, driving to the synagogue for prayer only; Israeli Masorti did not adopt the driving permission.
The Reform principle is informed choice: each person decides which practices will make their Shabbat holy and joyful.
Almost all rabbis advise taking on Shabbat in steps: dinner, synagogue, havdalah, refraining from weekday activities, a digital rest, full observance according to your movement.

blocks.text: What all the movements share

Orthodox, Conservative (Masorti) and Reform Judaism understand differently how binding the law is, but all three see Shabbat as the center of Jewish life. In every community you will find candle lighting, kiddush over wine, challot, Friday evening and Shabbat morning services, the reading of the weekly Torah portion, and havdalah. The movements differ on the question of prohibitions: what exactly counts as “work,” and who decides how Shabbat is to be kept — halacha handed down from generation to generation, or the informed choice of the individual and the community. To understand the beit din of your own movement and to respect other communities, it is helpful to know all three approaches.
The Orthodox approach

For Orthodox Judaism, the laws of Shabbat are binding halacha, set out in the Talmud and the codes (Shulchan Aruch, Kitzur Shulchan Aruch) and applied by contemporary halachic authorities to new situations. All 39 melachot with their derivatives and the rabbinic prohibitions are observed: people do not travel by vehicle, do not use electricity, phones or money, do not cook, do not write, and carry things only within an eruv. That is why Orthodox families live within walking distance of a synagogue. For an Orthodox beit din, full observance of Shabbat is one of the key conditions for giyur: the candidate must actually live by these laws, and the members of the beit din usually want to see that the candidate spends Shabbat within the community.
The Conservative approach: the 1950 responsum

The Conservative movement (Masorti) also regards halacha as binding, but holds that it develops historically and may be interpreted by authorized bodies. The main such body is the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards (CJLS) of the Rabbinical Assembly. In 1950 the committee adopted the famous “Responsum on the Sabbath” (its authors were Rabbis Morris Adler, Jacob Agus and Theodore Friedman). This decision was a response to a new reality: after the Second World War, American Jews moved en masse to the suburbs, far from synagogues, and many stopped coming to services.

items: Those who live too far away to walk **are permitted to drive to the synagogue** — only in order to take part in communal prayer, and not for any other purpose (not for shopping, not for visiting).
It is permitted **to use electric light** on Shabbat.
The goal is to strengthen communal life and to make Shabbat a source of spiritual renewal rather than of prohibitions that had become too heavy to bear.

blocks.text: This responsum has always been controversial even within the movement itself: many Conservative rabbis saw it as a reluctant concession and urged people to walk. The Israeli Masorti movement, where synagogues are usually close to home, did not adopt the permission to drive. For a Conservative candidate this means: Shabbat is kept as law — with kiddush, prayer, and refraining from work, commerce and weekday matters — but some technical questions are decided differently than in Orthodoxy.

differs.text: A Conservative beit din expects Shabbat observance according to Masorti norms: attending the Shabbat service, home rituals, and refraining from work and commerce; the specific requirements (driving, electrical appliances) depend on the rabbi and the community.

blocks.text: The Reform approach: informed choice

Classical Reform Judaism of the 19th century (the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885) declared that ritual laws “not adapted to the views and habits of modern civilization” are not binding. Some Reform communities at that time even moved their main service to Sunday. Later the movement returned to tradition: the CCAR (Central Conference of American Rabbis) published a Shabbat guide, “Gates of Shabbat,” and the 1999 “Statement of Principles” calls on Jews to study and observe the mitzvot, including sanctifying Shabbat.

Today the Reform principle is **informed choice**: a person studies the tradition and decides for themselves which practices will make their Shabbat holy, distinct from the weekdays, and joyful. This is not “less Shabbat” but a different source of commitment — personal autonomy and conscience rather than halachic command.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism the 39 melachot are not regarded as binding law: driving, electricity and cooking are acceptable as long as they do not disturb the rest and holiness of the day. Work is understood as weekday labor, business and shopping; Shabbat is built around rest, holiness and joy — candles, kiddush, the communal service, family and study.

blocks.text: Reform giyur programs (for example, in Saint Petersburg and Moscow) expect the candidate to take part regularly in the community’s Friday evening services, to learn the home rituals — candles, kiddush, havdalah — and to develop a personal, thoughtful relationship with the seventh day.
How a candidate can begin keeping Shabbat

No one starts keeping Shabbat in its full scope “as of Monday.” Almost all rabbis advise going step by step, adding something new every few weeks — but moving consistently forward. Here is a sample path:

items: **Friday night dinner.** Candles, kiddush, challot, festive food, the phone put away. Invite friends or family.
**Synagogue.** Go regularly to Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday and to the morning service on Shabbat; get to know the community.
**Havdalah.** See Shabbat out at home or in the community.
**Refraining from weekday activities.** Do not work, do not shop, do not clean or do household chores, do not answer work email.
**Digital rest.** Turn off your phone and computer for 25 hours — for many people this is the hardest and the most liberating step.

**Full observance according to your movement.** Studying the melachot with a mentor, preparing your home (timers, a hot plate, unscrewing the light bulb in the refrigerator), finding out whether there is an eruv.

blocks.text: For an Orthodox candidate: you will usually be required to live within walking distance of an Orthodox synagogue and to spend Shabbat regularly with observant families. There is also a subtle point: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 58b) says that a non-Jew should not keep Shabbat fully, since it is a sign of the covenant with Israel. That is why many Orthodox rabbis advise a candidate before giyur to keep Shabbat but deliberately perform one small act on it that is forbidden to a Jew. Exactly what and how is for your rabbi to decide; do not make it up yourself.

At the beit din you will almost certainly be asked how you spend Shabbat. Answer concretely and honestly: what time you light candles, who makes kiddush, which synagogue you attend, what has been hardest for you and what has changed. The members of the beit din value sincerity more than a perfect picture.

questions.prompt: Explain how the approaches of Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Judaism to Shabbat differ. How do you relate to communities of other movements?
questions.modelAnswer: All three movements consider Shabbat the center of Jewish life: candles, kiddush, challahs, services and havdalah are found everywhere. Orthodoxy observes all 39 melachot and the prohibitions of the Sages as binding halacha: no driving, no electricity. The Conservative movement considers halacha binding but evolving; the CJLS responsum of 1950 permitted driving to the synagogue for those who live far away and using electric light, although Masorti in Israel did not adopt driving. Reform Judaism proceeds from informed choice: a person chooses meaningful practices of rest, holiness and joy. I respect other communities and, when visiting, keep the rules accepted by my hosts.

Exactly what to do is decided by my rabbi; I follow his instruction. After giyur I will keep Shabbat in full.

questions.modelAnswer: You need a cup of wine or grape juice, spices and a candle with several wicks. Last is said “ha-mavdil bein kodesh le-chol” about the separation of the holy from the ordinary. Then the wine is drunk, the candle is extinguished, and “Shavua tov” is wished.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “The commandment of Shabbat is given in two words — ‘remember' and ‘keep'. Explain in your own words what each of them means and how you fulfill both in your life?”
questions.modelAnswer: According to the Talmud, “remember” and “keep” were spoken in a single utterance, and tradition sees in this two sides of one day. “Remember” is what I do: I light the candles, recite kiddush, gather the family at the festive table, sing and rejoice in the Sabbath. “Keep” is what I refrain from: on Shabbat I do not work, do not shop and set aside the phone, so that the ordinary does not disturb the holiness of the day. For me these two sides are inseparable: the day is sanctified both by action and by restraint. So I both welcome Shabbat worthily and guard it from the weekdays.
