questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “Tell us about lighting the Shabbat candles: when and how do you do it, why are at least two candles lit, and what does this moment mean to you?”
questions.modelAnswer: On Friday I check the candle-lighting time in advance and light the candles eighteen minutes before sunset — as accepted by the widespread custom. I light at least two candles — in memory of the two words of the commandment, “remember” and “keep”; in many families a candle is added for each child. I recite the blessing “lehadlik ner shel Shabbat”, and then stand before the flames for a few minutes and pray in my own words. The Talmud connects the candles with shalom bayit — peace in the home — and for me this ritual is the heart of welcoming Shabbat: by candlelight the ordinary week ends and holy time begins.
keyPoints: Two candles — in memory of the words “remember” and “keep”
Candles are lit before sunset, usually 18 minutes before
The blessing “lehadlik ner shel Shabbat”
Candles — shalom bayit, peace in the home
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate knows the meaning and order of lighting the candles and invests it with personal meaning.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 23b (quoted in the lesson)

differs.text: In Reform communities the candles are often lit in the synagogue at the beginning of the service or at home at the beginning of the dinner, even after sunset.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “Imagine that on Friday evening you are invited to dinner at relatives who do not keep Shabbat. What will you do?”
questions.modelAnswer: I will not lecture my loved ones or turn dinner into an argument: peace with family is part of Shabbat for me. I will ask in advance what time everyone sits down at the table. If the sun has not yet set, I will offer to light candles; if Shabbat has already begun, I will not light a flame, but, if the hosts do not mind, I will recite kiddush over wine or juice and “ha-motzi” over two challahs. I will set aside the phone, not talk about work, and not ask anyone to do for me what I do not do on Shabbat. If some step of the meal does not work out, I will let it go without reproach, but I will not violate Shabbat for convenience. I will explain the meaning of the day briefly and warmly, but only if asked.
keyPoints: Do not judge relatives or start an argument
Candles — only before sunset; kiddush and “ha-motzi” can be recited even at someone else's table
Phone set aside, no talk of work, no asking others to do melachah for you
Flexibility in the order of the meal without violating Shabbat
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether the candidate can keep both his Shabbat and peace with loved ones, without judging their home.
questions.source: Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 77; Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 106a (quoted in the lesson)

differs.text: In Reform communities the candles are often lit at the beginning of the dinner, even after sunset, and what to refrain from on Shabbat each person decides consciously.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “Tell us how you yourself keep Shabbat: what you refrain from, how you handle work, the phone and travel, and what is hardest for you?”
questions.modelAnswer: On Shabbat I do not work and do not answer work email, do not shop and do not use money. I prepare food before Shabbat and do not cook on the day itself; I set aside the phone and computer — honestly, that was the hardest and the most liberating step. I make no trips for errands: I walk to the synagogue, and I build the day around prayer, meals with loved ones and Torah study. If I am unsure whether something is permitted, I ask my rabbi rather than look for a leniency. When it is a matter of life and health, I do not delay: pikuach nefesh takes precedence over Shabbat, and to help is a mitzvah.
keyPoints: No work and no answering work matters on Shabbat
No cooking, shopping or use of money
Phone and computer set aside; walking to the synagogue, no trips for errands
Pikuach nefesh — life takes precedence over Shabbat prohibitions
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at what the candidate actually refrains from, how he resolves the question of travel, and whether he delays when a life must be saved.
questions.source: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 328:2 (quoted in the lesson)

differs.text: A Reform beit din expects a concrete account of your Shabbat: candles, kiddush, services, family, refraining from weekday work and shopping if you have accepted that. You need to be able to explain the 39 melachot, but the judges do not require that you already live by all their details. Say honestly what you keep, what you are still learning and why this day is holy to you.

A Conservative beit din expects observance of Shabbat according to Masorti norms: services, home rituals, refraining from work and commerce; driving to the synagogue and electric light may be acceptable — check the standard with your rabbi.
An Orthodox beit din expects full observance of the laws of Shabbat, living within walking distance of a synagogue and living experience of Shabbat in observant families.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “Why does Shabbat not simply end but is escorted by a separate ritual? What does havdalah mean to you?”
questions.modelAnswer: According to Rambam, the commandment “remember the Shabbat day to sanctify it” means sanctifying Shabbat with words both on entering — with kiddush — and on leaving — with havdalah. For me these are the two frames of one holy time: a day welcomed ceremoniously is not cut off but escorted with honor, like a guest. When the blessing about the separation of the holy from the ordinary is said, I say farewell to the Sabbath: the “additional soul” departs, the fragrance of the spices revives the soul, and the fire recalls how Adam obtained flame at the close of the first Shabbat: on weekdays one may create again. Then we sing “Eliyahu ha-Navi” and wish each other “Shavua tov”; in many families a Melavveh Malkah follows. Into the new week I try to enter rested and with peace in the home.
keyPoints: Havdalah — the sanctification of the departure of Shabbat, the counterpart of kiddush (the Rambam)
The spices revive the soul at the departure of the “additional soul”; the fire is Adam's flame
“Eliyahu HaNavi,” “Shavua tov,” and, for many, melaveh malkah
Personal: to enter the weekdays rested, and with peace in the home
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether the candidate understands the meaning of havdalah as the close of holy time, and whether the candidate carries its mood into the weekdays.
questions.source: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Shabbat 29:1 (quoted in the lesson)

questions.prompt: What does the root sh-b-t, from which the word “Shabbat” comes, mean?
questions.explanation: The word “Shabbat” comes from the root sh-b-t — “to cease and to stop”: on the seventh day the Almighty ceased to create.
questions.source: Lesson: The meaning of Shabbat: creation, freedom, and the covenant

questions.prompt: When does Shabbat begin?
options: On Friday night, exactly at midnight
questions.explanation: Shabbat begins on Friday evening at sunset and ends on Saturday when the stars appear.
questions.source: Lesson: The meaning of Shabbat: creation, freedom, and the covenant

questions.prompt: Why is Friday evening already considered Shabbat?
options: Because the sages so ruled, for the sake of tosefet Shabbat
Because candles are lit on Friday evening
Because the Jewish day begins in the evening: “and there was evening and there was morning”
questions.explanation: The Jewish day always begins in the evening, as in the account of Creation: “and there was evening and there was morning — one day”; therefore Friday evening is already the seventh day.

questions.prompt: Which Jewish thinker called Shabbat “a palace in time”?
questions.explanation: The philosopher Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel called Shabbat “a palace in time”: a sanctuary is built not of stone, but of hours given to the Almighty, to family, and to the soul.
questions.source: Lesson: The meaning of Shabbat: creation, freedom, and the covenant

questions.prompt: To what does the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch (72:1) equate a person who violates Shabbat?
options: To one who has violated only a prohibition of the sages
To one who denies the entire Torah
To one who has committed a minor offense
To one who is exempt from the mitzvot
questions.explanation: According to the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch (72:1), keeping Shabbat is testimony to faith in the Creator, and one who violates Shabbat is equated with one who denies the entire Torah.

questions.prompt: It is customary to fast on Shabbat in order to emphasize the holiness of the day.
questions.explanation: Shabbat is a day of delight (oneg Shabbat): one does not fast on Shabbat, except when Yom Kippur falls on Saturday.

questions.prompt: The words “More than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews” belong to Ahad Ha'am.
questions.explanation: This statement is from an essay on Shabbat by Ahad Ha'am (Asher Ginsberg), 1898.
questions.source: Ahad Ha'am (Asher Ginsberg), essay on Shabbat (1898)

questions.prompt: Match each passage in the Tanakh with what it says about Shabbat.
pairs: G-d blessed and sanctified the seventh day
Shabbat is a sign and an eternal covenant
questions.explanation: These verses are the main sources of the lesson: the sanctification of the seventh day at Creation, the two records of the commandment, the covenant, and the prophet's words about oneg Shabbat.

questions.prompt: What are the Ten Commandments called in Hebrew — the “ten utterances”?
questions.explanation: The Ten Commandments in Hebrew are “Aseret HaDibrot,” the “ten utterances”; the commandment of Shabbat is the fourth of them.
questions.source: Lesson: The meaning of Shabbat: creation, freedom, and the covenant

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “The Torah calls Shabbat a sign between the Almighty and the people of Israel. How does this sign show itself in your life?”
questions.modelAnswer: The Torah calls Shabbat an “ot” — a sign — and a “brit olam,” an eternal covenant (Shemot 31:16–17); it uses the same word “ot” for brit milah as well. For me this is a visible sign of an inner bond: colleagues and friends know that from Friday evening until the stars appear on Saturday I cannot be reached and I do not work. Every Friday, as I light the candles and listen to kiddush, I feel that I belong to a people that has kept this covenant for thousands of years. The words of Ahad Ha'am are close to my heart: not only have the Jews kept Shabbat, but Shabbat has kept the Jews. I want my home to become a link in this chain.
keyPoints: Shemot 31:16–17: “ot” (a sign) and “brit olam” (an eternal covenant)
The sign is visible to others: on Shabbat I do not work and cannot be reached
A personal bond with the people of Israel and the Creator
questions.explanation: A good answer draws on the verses of “Veshamru” and shows how keeping Shabbat is visible in the candidate's everyday life.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “What is menuchah? How does your Shabbat differ from an ordinary day off?”
questions.modelAnswer: On an ordinary day off, people manage to do the shopping, the cleaning, and the tasks they did not get to during the week. Menuchah is different: on Shabbat I produce nothing and I change nothing in the world; I simply live in it. I pray, have dinner with my loved ones, take a walk, read, and study the weekly Torah portion, and I try not to talk about business or about sad things. The prophet Yeshayahu tells us to call Shabbat a delight and to honor it, so I prepare the home and festive clothing in advance. In this way I acknowledge that the world belongs to the Creator, and not to me.
keyPoints: Menuchah is rest and harmony, not idleness
Creating nothing and changing nothing in the world
Oneg and kavod Shabbat (Yeshayahu 58:13)
questions.explanation: The lesson explains menuchah as inner peace and harmony, not simply rest; to it are added oneg (delight) and kavod (honor) of Shabbat.

questions.prompt: What do Ashkenazim call the traditional hot dish for Shabbat lunch?
questions.explanation: The hot Shabbat dish among Ashkenazim is cholent; among Sephardim it is called chamin or dafina.
questions.source: Lesson: Preparing for and welcoming Shabbat: candles and Kabbalat Shabbat

questions.prompt: What do the worshippers do during the last stanza of “Lecha Dodi” — “Bo'i veshalom”?
options: They stand, turn toward the synagogue entrance, and bow
They sit and cover their eyes with their palms
They leave the synagogue for a field to meet the sunset
They raise a cup of wine and recite the blessing
questions.explanation: At the stanza “Bo'i veshalom” (“Come in peace”) they stand and turn toward the entrance, as if welcoming the Shabbat bride as she enters, and they bow.

questions.prompt: Which psalms open Kabbalat Shabbat in the Ashkenazi rite — one for each weekday?
questions.explanation: In the Ashkenazi rite, Kabbalat Shabbat opens with six psalms — 95, 96, 97, 98, 99, and 29, one for each weekday; psalms 92 and 93 are read after “Lecha Dodi.”

questions.prompt: From what time, according to halacha, may one accept Shabbat before sunset?
options: No earlier than 18 minutes before sunset
From plag haminchah — about an hour and a quarter of “seasonal” hours before sunset
questions.explanation: One may accept Shabbat early beginning from plag haminchah (about an hour and a quarter of “seasonal” hours before sunset); one who has accepted Shabbat is already obligated to observe all its prohibitions.
questions.source: Lesson: Preparing for and welcoming Shabbat: candles and Kabbalat Shabbat

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, the great sages assigned the preparations for Shabbat to servants and took no part in them themselves.
questions.explanation: The Talmud tells that the great scholars prepared for Shabbat with their own hands: they cut vegetables, chopped wood, lit the stove, and carried the groceries.

questions.prompt: On the eve of Shabbat, Rabbi Chanina would put on his finest clothes and say: “Come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen.”
questions.explanation: So the Talmud tells it; Rabbi Yannai, for his part, would say “Come, O bride!” — the Kabbalat Shabbat service later grew out of these images.

questions.prompt: Many Sephardim, following the Shulchan Aruch, first light the Shabbat candles and only then recite the blessing.
questions.explanation: That is what Ashkenazim do (they light, cover their eyes, and recite the blessing); many Sephardim, following the Shulchan Aruch, recite the blessing before lighting.
questions.source: Lesson: Preparing for and welcoming Shabbat: candles and Kabbalat Shabbat

questions.prompt: Match each part of the preparation for Shabbat with what it includes.
pairs: Everything that needs to be cooked is cooked before Shabbat
A white tablecloth, candlesticks, two challot under a napkin
A shower, trimming the nails, festive clothing
Pay the bills, notify colleagues, set the phone aside
Coins in a tzedakah box before the candles are lit
questions.explanation: The lesson lists these five sides of preparation as part of kavod Shabbat — the honoring of Shabbat.
questions.source: Lesson: Preparing for and welcoming Shabbat: candles and Kabbalat Shabbat

questions.prompt: What is the name of the hymn (“Come, my friend”) with which the Shabbat bride is welcomed at Kabbalat Shabbat?
questions.explanation: “Lecha Dodi” means “Come, my friend, to meet the bride”; in the hymn the groom is the people of Israel, and the bride is Shabbat.
questions.source: Siddur, Kabbalat Shabbat (the refrain of “Lecha Dodi”)

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “The sages of the Talmud prepared for Shabbat with their own hands. Why is preparation part of the mitzvah, and what do you yourself do for Shabbat?”
questions.modelAnswer: Preparation is part of kavod Shabbat, the honoring of Shabbat. The sages said: “One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat,” and the Talmud tells that even the great scholars themselves cut vegetables and chopped wood. So I do not leave it all to others: on Friday, with my own hands, I prepare the food, tidy the house, and cover the table with a white cloth, and I set out the candlesticks and two challot. Ahead of time I finish my work and tell my colleagues that I will be unreachable. When everything is ready before sunset, I welcome Shabbat calmly, and not in a rush.
keyPoints: Preparation is kavod Shabbat
“One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat…” (Avodah Zarah 3a); the sages prepared themselves (Shabbat 119a)
Concrete tasks: food, the home, clothing, work matters
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that no position exempts a person from serving Shabbat personally; the answer must be concrete.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “In the synagogue on Friday evening, Shabbat is welcomed as a bride and a queen. Where does this image come from, and how do you experience the Kabbalat Shabbat service?”
questions.modelAnswer: This image comes from the Talmud: Rabbi Chanina said, “Come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen,” and Rabbi Yannai, “Come, O bride!” The kabbalists of Tzfat in the 16th century shaped the Kabbalat Shabbat service out of these words. In “Lecha Dodi” the groom is the people of Israel and the bride is Shabbat, and at the last stanza we stand and turn toward the entrance, as if welcoming her. For me this is the moment when the week is left behind: I come to the synagogue, sing together with everyone, and feel that Shabbat has truly entered my life.
keyPoints: Shabbat 119a: the Queen and the bride
Kabbalat Shabbat — Tzfat, the 16th century; “Lecha Dodi”
A personal experience of welcoming Shabbat
questions.explanation: The answer links the Talmudic image of the bride and the queen with the Kabbalat Shabbat service and adds a personal experience.

questions.prompt: With what words are daughters blessed on Friday evening?
options: “May G-d make you like Ephraim and Menashe”
“May G-d make you like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah”
“A Woman of Valor — who can find her?”
questions.explanation: Daughters are blessed with the words “May G-d make you like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah”; sons — “Ephraim and Menashe.”
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: What is the Shabbat challah sprinkled with after the blessing “Hamotzi”?
questions.explanation: The cut challah is sprinkled with salt — as the offerings in the Temple were salted; tradition compares the table to the altar.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: What, in most communities, follows immediately after kiddush?
questions.explanation: The order is this: “Shalom Aleichem,” “Eshet Chayil,” the blessing of the children, kiddush, then the washing of the hands and “Hamotzi”; only in some communities (for example, among German Jews) is the washing done before kiddush.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

differs.text: In Reform practice, the ritual washing of the hands before bread is usually not considered obligatory: after kiddush, the bread is often blessed right away.

questions.prompt: Who composed the Aramaic Shabbat hymn “Yah Ribon Olam” (“Master of the World”)?
questions.explanation: The hymn “Yah Ribon Olam” was composed by Rabbi Yisrael Najara in the 16th century; it is sung among the zemirot at the Shabbat table.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: Over what, according to halacha, is the evening Shabbat kiddush recited if there is neither wine nor grape juice?
options: In that case kiddush is canceled
questions.explanation: Grape juice is equal to wine for kiddush. If there is neither wine nor juice, the evening kiddush is recited over the two challot; chamar medinah, by Ashkenazi custom, is permitted only for the morning kiddush.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 271; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 77

questions.prompt: If one person recites kiddush and the others listen and answer “amen,” they too fulfill the mitzvah.
questions.explanation: One person recites kiddush for everyone, and those who listen, by answering “amen,” fulfill the mitzvah; women may recite kiddush for others as well.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: According to halacha, one may recite kiddush in one place and eat the meal itself later in another home.
questions.explanation: The rule “kiddush bimkom seudah” applies: kiddush is valid only in the place of the meal, and one eats right after it.
questions.source: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 271; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 77

questions.prompt: Match each element of the Shabbat meal with its description.
pairs: A greeting to the ministering angels
Two whole challot on the table
An insertion about Shabbat rest in Birkat Hamazon
questions.explanation: All these elements are part of the order of the Friday night dinner described in the lesson.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: What is the third Shabbat meal, eaten toward Saturday evening, called?
questions.explanation: The third meal of Shabbat, toward Saturday evening, is called seudah shlishit.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “What goes on at your Shabbat table besides the food — which songs do you sing, and what do you talk about?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me the Shabbat table is a little like the altar in the Temple: on it are candles, challot, salt, and wine. Between the courses we sing zemirot — for example, “Yom Zeh Mechubad” or “Yah Ribon Olam,” which Rabbi Yisrael Najara composed. I try to share something from the weekly Torah portion, so that the meal becomes a lesson as well, and the guests share their thoughts too. The phones are set aside. We finish with the blessing after the meal: before it we sing “Shir Hama'alot,” and we add the insertion “Retzeh” to the text.
keyPoints: Zemirot — Shabbat songs
Words of Torah from the weekly portion
Birkat Hamazon with the insertion “Retzeh” and “Shir Hama'alot”
questions.explanation: The lesson describes zemirot, words of Torah at the table, and Birkat Hamazon with the insertion “Retzeh” as parts of the Shabbat meal that turn it into a lesson and a celebration.
questions.source: Lesson: The Shabbat meal: kiddush, challot, and zemirot

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “Do you have a custom of blessing the children on Friday evening? How is it done, and what is said?”
questions.modelAnswer: After “Shalom Aleichem” and “Eshet Chayil,” the parents place their hands on the children's heads and bless them. Sons are blessed with the words of Yaakov: “May G-d make you like Ephraim and Menashe,” and daughters — “May G-d make you like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah.” Then the Priestly Blessing is recited: “May the L-rd bless you and keep you…”. In the family where I often spend Shabbat, this is the warmest moment of the evening, and the children wait for it all week. For me it is a reminder that Shabbat is passed from generation to generation through the family.
keyPoints: Hands on the child's head, before kiddush
Sons — Ephraim and Menashe; daughters — Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, Leah
The Priestly Blessing (Bamidbar 6:24–26)
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the blessing of the children as the third part of the Friday night dinner, before kiddush, with the Priestly Blessing.

questions.prompt: What does the verse Shemot 35:3 directly forbid?
options: Kindling a fire in all dwellings on the Shabbat day
questions.explanation: The verse says: “Do not kindle a fire in all your dwellings on the Shabbat day.”

questions.prompt: Which of the following is done at once on Shabbat, for the sake of pikuach nefesh?
options: Preparing a hot lunch for guests
Fixing a faucet that drips slightly
Taking a woman in labor to the hospital
questions.explanation: Calling an ambulance, taking a woman in labor to the hospital, and giving a necessary medicine when life is in danger are done at once; the rest has nothing to do with saving a life.
questions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 328:2

questions.prompt: Of which primary melachah is squeezing juice from fruit considered a derivative (toladah)?
questions.explanation: Squeezing juice is a derivative of “threshing”: in both cases one separates the contents from the shell.
questions.source: Lesson: The 39 types of work, muktzeh, the eruv, and pikuach nefesh

questions.prompt: What is shevut?
options: A protective prohibition of the sages (for example, not trading)
A derivative act of a primary melachah
A symbolic fence around a neighborhood
The time between sunset and the stars
questions.explanation: Shevut means protective prohibitions established by the sages: not discussing weekday matters, not trading, and not asking a non-Jew to perform a melachah.
questions.source: Lesson: The 39 types of work, muktzeh, the eruv, and pikuach nefesh

questions.prompt: The Torah itself directly lists all 39 types of work forbidden on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: The Torah forbids “all work,” but does not list its types; the sages derived them from the building of the Mishkan, and the Mishnah gave the list.

questions.prompt: Food, dishes, books, and clothing are muktzeh, so on Shabbat they may not be moved.
questions.explanation: Food, dishes, books, and clothing are not muktzeh; muktzeh is, for example, money, stones, tools for forbidden work, and a candlestick with a flame.

questions.prompt: The measure of the distance one may go beyond the city on Shabbat — 2000 cubits — is connected with the eruv techumin.
questions.explanation: The lesson connects the eruv techumin with the permitted distance beyond the city and gives the measure as 2000 cubits.
questions.source: Lesson: The 39 types of work, muktzeh, the eruv, and pikuach nefesh

questions.prompt: Match each halachic term with its meaning.
pairs: A private domain: an enclosed house and yard
A public domain: a major street
“The form of a doorway” — the enclosure of an eruv
It allows food to be cooked on a festival for Shabbat
questions.explanation: Halacha distinguishes three kinds of domains; an eruv is built of enclosures in the “form of a doorway,” and eruv tavshilin relates to preparing food on a festival.
questions.source: Lesson: The 39 types of work, muktzeh, the eruv, and pikuach nefesh

questions.prompt: What are the objects called that the sages forbade moving on Shabbat (Heb. “set aside”)?
questions.explanation: Muktzeh (“set aside”) — things that are not moved on Shabbat, so as not to come to a melachah and so that the day does not resemble a weekday.

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: “On Shabbat your neighbor suddenly has severe chest pain. What will you do? What is your decision based on?”
questions.modelAnswer: I will immediately call an ambulance and do everything needed to save him, without waiting for Shabbat to end and without losing time on questions. This is pikuach nefesh — the saving of a life, for the sake of which it is not merely permitted but obligatory to break Shabbat. The Torah says of the mitzvot: “…which a person shall do and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5), and the Sages add: “live by them, and not die because of them” (Yoma 85b). Even if it is unclear whether there is real danger, a doubt about a threat to life also obligates one to act. The Shulchan Aruch praises the one who hurries, and of the one who delays with questions it says that he sheds blood (Orach Chaim 328:2).
keyPoints: Pikuach nefesh: breaking Shabbat is obligatory
Vayikra 18:5 and Yoma 85b
When in doubt — act as in a case of danger
Whoever hurries is worthy of praise (Orach Chaim 328:2)
questions.explanation: The answer should show that saving a life outweighs Shabbat, and should name the sources and the rule about doubt.
questions.source: Vayikra 18:5; Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 328:2

questions.prompt: When does Shabbat end?
options: When three medium-sized stars are visible in the sky
questions.explanation: Shabbat ends on Saturday evening, when three medium-sized stars are visible (tzeit hakochavim), usually 40–50 minutes after sunset.

questions.prompt: About how long does Shabbat last from its beginning until the stars come out?
questions.explanation: Shabbat begins before sunset on Friday and ends only when the stars come out on Saturday — so it lasts more than a full day, about 25 hours.

questions.prompt: Whose opinion underlies the custom of many Chassidim to wait 72 minutes after sunset before Shabbat ends?
questions.explanation: Many Chassidim and some other communities wait 72 minutes, following the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam.

questions.prompt: Until when may havdalah be made up if it was not done on Saturday evening?
options: Until the end of Sunday, with all the blessings
Until the end of Tuesday, but without the candle and the spices
questions.explanation: A missed havdalah may be made up until the end of Tuesday, but then without the blessings over the candle and the spices.

questions.prompt: After havdalah people sing the song “Eliyahu HaNavi” about the prophet who, according to tradition, will come to announce the redemption.
questions.explanation: After havdalah people sing “Eliyahu HaNavi” and wish each other “Shavua tov!”.

questions.prompt: If Shabbat leads directly into a festival, havdalah is included in the festival kiddush, and spices are not used.
questions.explanation: The lesson says so: when Shabbat passes into a festival, havdalah is included in the festival kiddush, without spices.

questions.prompt: Match each havdalah blessing with what it is said over.
pairs: The main blessing over the cup, at the end
questions.explanation: The order of havdalah is wine, spices, the candle, and at the end the blessing of separation, again over the cup.
questions.source: Siddur, havdalah; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 297–298

questions.prompt: What is the Hebrew name of the spices that are smelled at havdalah?
questions.explanation: The spices for havdalah are besamim (b'samim): cloves, cinnamon, myrtle, or a spice box.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the prayer of separation inserted into the fourth blessing of the Amidah in the evening service at the departure of Shabbat?
questions.explanation: In the Maariv at the departure of Shabbat, the prayer of separation “Atah chonantanu” is inserted into the fourth blessing of the Amidah.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “How does your evening after havdalah go? What do ‘Shavua tov’ and melaveh malkah mean?”
questions.modelAnswer: After havdalah we sing “Eliyahu HaNavi” — a song about the prophet who, according to tradition, will come to announce the redemption. Then we wish each other “Shavua tov!” — “A good week!” — so that the light of Shabbat passes into the weekdays. Sometimes we hold a melaveh malkah — a small meal of “escorting the Queen,” which tradition connects with King David. In this way we escort Shabbat out with honor, like a dear guest seen to the door. This helps me begin the week not in a rush, but with the sense that Shabbat continues to shine.
keyPoints: “Eliyahu HaNavi” after havdalah
“Shavua tov” — a good week
Melaveh malkah — escorting the Queen
questions.explanation: The lesson describes that after havdalah people sing “Eliyahu HaNavi,” wish each other “Shavua tov,” and hold a melaveh malkah.

questions.prompt: What is found in the communities of all three movements — Orthodox, Conservative and Reform?
options: A Shabbat elevator and Shabbat timers
Lighting candles, kiddush, challot and havdalah
The main service of the week on Sunday
questions.explanation: All the movements see Shabbat as the center of Jewish life: candles, kiddush, challot, services, Torah reading and havdalah are found in every community.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

questions.prompt: According to the sample path in the lesson, what is the best way to begin keeping Shabbat?
options: With Friday night dinner: candles, kiddush, challot
With giving up all 39 melachot at once
With studying all the laws of the eruv
With turning the phone off for the whole week
questions.explanation: The first step is Friday night dinner: candles, kiddush, challot, festive food and the phone put away; the rest is added gradually.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

questions.prompt: Why do Orthodox families usually live within walking distance of a synagogue?
options: Because travel by vehicle is forbidden on Shabbat
Because an eruv is in effect only near the synagogue
Because one may not pray at home on Shabbat
Because the Pittsburgh Platform requires it
questions.explanation: Orthodoxy keeps all the melachot and does not travel by vehicle on Shabbat, so people walk to the synagogue.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

questions.prompt: Who were the authors of the CJLS “Responsum on the Sabbath” of 1950?
options: Rabbis Morris Adler, Jacob Agus and Theodore Friedman
Rabbis Abraham Joshua Heschel and Hayim Donin
The Chazon Ish and Rav Chaim Naeh
The compilers of “Gates of Shabbat” from the CCAR
questions.explanation: The 1950 responsum was written by Rabbis Morris Adler, Jacob Agus and Theodore Friedman.

differs.text: Within the Conservative movement the responsum was controversial; Israeli Masorti did not adopt the permission to drive. Orthodoxy does not recognize this decision.

questions.prompt: Almost all rabbis advise beginning to keep Shabbat gradually, adding something new every few weeks.
questions.explanation: One does not begin Shabbat all at once, in its full scope: one goes step by step, but steadily and forward.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

questions.prompt: The 1950 CJLS responsum permitted driving a car on Shabbat not only to the synagogue, but also on visits or to go shopping.
questions.explanation: The permission applied only to the drive to the synagogue for communal prayer, for those who live too far away — not for shopping and not for visits.

questions.prompt: Match each document with its content.
pairs: Ritual laws that do not accord with the views of modern civilization are not binding
Driving to the synagogue for prayer, and electric light
The CCAR guide to Shabbat observance
A call to study and observe the mitzvot, and to sanctify Shabbat
questions.explanation: The lesson traces the path of Reform Judaism from the Pittsburgh Platform to a return to tradition, and the Conservative decision of 1950.
questions.source: Pittsburgh Platform (1885); CJLS, “A Responsum on the Sabbath” (1950); “A Statement of Principles for Reform Judaism,” CCAR (Pittsburgh, 1999)

questions.prompt: Which tractate of the Talmud says that a non-Jew should not keep Shabbat fully?
questions.explanation: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 58b) says that a non-Jew should not keep Shabbat fully, for it is a sign of the covenant with Israel.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Why is it important to us to see that you spend Shabbat in the community? How does this happen for you?”
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that Shabbat cannot be learned from books alone: its laws live in the community and in families that keep them from generation to generation. For an Orthodox beit din, full observance of Shabbat is one of the key conditions of giyur, and it must be clear that I live this way in practice. That is why I live within walking distance of the synagogue and go to Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday and to the morning service on Saturday. I often spend Shabbat with an observant family: I see how the home is prepared in advance, how kiddush and havdalah are made, and how they manage without electricity. Details I do not understand, I clarify with my rabbi.
keyPoints: Full observance of Shabbat is a key condition of Orthodox giyur
Walking distance from the synagogue, services on Friday and Saturday
Shabbat with observant families, questions for the rabbi
questions.explanation: The lesson says that an Orthodox beit din wants to see the candidate living by the laws of Shabbat in the community and near the synagogue.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

differs.text: A Conservative beit din expects Shabbat observance according to Masorti norms; the requirements for driving and electrical appliances depend on the rabbi and the community.
Reform giyur schools expect regular participation in Friday evening services, learning candles, kiddush and havdalah, and a personal, thoughtful relationship with Shabbat.

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “Many people say that the hardest thing on Shabbat is giving up the phone. How do you manage this?”
questions.modelAnswer: Digital rest — turning off the phone and the computer for 25 hours — turned out, for me, to be the hardest and the most liberating step. Before the candles are lit I answer important messages and tell my family and colleagues that I will be out of reach until the stars come out on Saturday. Then I turn the phone off and put it well away. For the first weeks this was unfamiliar, but now on Shabbat I have time for prayer, for those close to me, for books and for walks. I notice that this rest changes my week as well: I am calmer and less dependent on the screen.
keyPoints: Digital rest is one of the steps toward observance
Tell family and colleagues in advance
The time that is freed — prayer, family, study
questions.explanation: In the lesson, digital rest is called the hardest and the most liberating step on the path to keeping Shabbat.
questions.source: Lesson: Shabbat in the different movements, and how to begin keeping it

questions.prompt: What is the role of the prophet Eliyahu in relation to Mashiach?
options: Eliyahu will come before Mashiach and prepare hearts
Eliyahu will come after Mashiach has finished his work
Eliyahu has already come and announced that Mashiach has been
questions.explanation: Eliyahu will yet come before Mashiach, who is awaited, and will prepare the hearts of the people. This is how Malachi 3:23 and the Rambam (Laws of Kings 12:2) are read.

questions.prompt: How does Reform Judaism relate to the 39 melachot?
options: They are to be known as the language of the tradition, but they are not regarded as a binding legal code
Every Reform Jew must keep them to the same extent as an Orthodox Jew
Teaching about them in class is forbidden, so as not to complicate life
They concern only the building of the Temple and have nothing to do with Shabbat
questions.explanation: The holiness of the day is built through rest, prayer, family and refraining from weekday labor, and not through the binding force of all the fences.
questions.source: Lesson “39 kinds of work…”; CCAR materials

questions.prompt: Why, in many Reform communities, is the main service of the week precisely Friday evening?
options: Kabbalat Shabbat gathers the community to welcome the day: candles, prayer, singing together, often with men and women taking part equally
Because on Saturday morning Reform Jews are forbidden to leave the house
Because the Torah forbids prayer on Saturday morning
Because a beit din accepts giyur only on Fridays
questions.explanation: The Friday service is the community’s welcoming of Shabbat; the table at home is not cancelled by this.
questions.source: Lesson on Shabbat in the different movements

questions.prompt: If a Reform Jew drives to the synagogue on Shabbat, that automatically means Shabbat is not holy for that person.
questions.explanation: Driving to services is usually not considered a violation in Reform practice. The holiness of the day is measured by rest, prayer and refraining from weekday bustle, and not by a copy of all 39 melachot.
questions.source: Lesson on the melachot, the section on the Reform view

questions.prompt: How do you build the holiness of Shabbat in Reform practice (or in another practice of your own)? What do you already keep every week, what are you still learning, and how do you understand the classic 39 melachot in this?
questions.modelAnswer: I can explain the 39 melachot: they are categories of creative work that the sages derived from the building of the Mishkan, and the language in which the tradition speaks about rest. In my Reform practice they are not a binding code, but I do not pretend that they do not exist. My Shabbat in practice looks like this: candles and kiddush, the community service, time with those close to me, refraining from work and shopping, quiet without the weekday bustle. I do not regard driving to the synagogue or using lights as a violation. I want to deepen this rhythm, and not stop at the minimum of “coming once a month.”
keyPoints: Be able to explain the 39 melachot as the language of the tradition
A concrete weekly rhythm: candles, kiddush, a service, rest
Honestly name what you do not accept as a legal code
Show growth, and not a one-time formality
questions.explanation: At the beit din a living account of your own day is valued, and not someone else’s norms presented as your own.
questions.source: Lessons on the melachot and on Shabbat in the movements

differs.text: An Orthodox beit din expects the melachot to be kept in practice, and not only the ability to retell them.
A Conservative beit din proceeds from Shabbat being binding according to Masorti norms; electricity and driving to the synagogue may be permitted by responsa.

questions.prompt: Shabbat can be moved to another day of the week if that is more convenient for the community.
questions.explanation: Shabbat is the seventh day, an eternal sign (Shemot 31:16–17). It is not moved.

questions.prompt: Why is Shabbat celebrated precisely on the seventh day?
options: It is an accidental custom, which can be shifted
Because on this day the Almighty ceased creating, and so it stands in the Torah
Because that is more convenient for the market and for the calendars of neighboring peoples
Because the sages chose a day different from the weekdays, with no connection to creation
questions.explanation: Bereshit 2:1–3 and Shemot 20:8–11 connect rest precisely with the seventh day of creation.
